article_content: By Emma Reynolds. PUBLISHED: 08:02 EST, 25 October 2012. | UPDATED: 10:03 EST, 25 October 2012. While most carve pumpkins with knives this Halloween, 'Wild' Bill Hickok prefers a different approach - using his Colt 1911 handgun as his primary tool. This dramatic video shows Hickok from Nashville, Tennessee, firing rounds into a pumpkin to create a spooky Halloween decoration. The video demonstrates how Hickok systematically shoots eye, nose, and mouth holes into the pumpkin, resulting in a lopsided grin with a 'rotting tooth' effect. With nearly 200,000 views on his YouTube channel, the clip features Hickok declaring 'it's pumpkin carving time again' before demonstrating his method. The historic Colt 1911, introduced in 1911 by John Browning, remains widely used globally. After shooting, Hickok jokes about the pumpkin's 'face' on both sides and concludes with 'Happy Halloween!' His extreme pumpkin destruction series includes methods like crushing with motorcycles and sledgehammers, unlikely to appear in family carving sessions.

article_content: HONG KONG - Guam captain Jason Cunliffe leads his team into the decisive second leg of their World Cup qualifier against Singapore on Tuesday, aiming for a victory that could transcend sports and amplify Guam's global profile. The U.S. territory, home to 170,000 residents and two major military bases (Andersen Air Force Base and Naval Base Guam), faces the Southeast Asian powerhouse seeking to overturn a 2-1 deficit from the first leg. Ranked 201st globally, Guam draws inspiration from their 2018 qualifying campaign where they stunned India (2-1) and Turkmenistan (1-0). Beyond soccer ambitions, Cunliffe sees the match as a platform to educate audiences about Guam's unique political status and cultural identity. 'We’re a U.S. territory often misunderstood,' said Cunliffe, whose late free-kick narrowed the gap. 'Americans rarely recognize us, but fans in places like India already know who we are. Every match is a chance to redefine perceptions.' Hosting on home soil after a two-year hiatus due to pandemic restrictions, Cunliffe highlights the importance of competitive matches for team development. A veteran since 2006, he connects Guam’s football journey to broader aspirations: 'We fly our own flag, sing our anthem—but politically, we’re overlooked. We want accountability alongside our strategic military value.' Born on Guam grants U.S. citizenship, yet residents lack voting rights or Senate representation, fostering feelings of disenfranchisement. 'Our priority is maintaining military bases while gaining self-determination,' Cunliffe insists. 'I’m Chamorro first—a reminder that identity matters more than geography.'

article_content: At 19, Lauren Hill of Lawrenceburg, Indiana, will realize her dream of playing college basketball in her first game – despite facing terminal illness. Diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor shortly after committing to Mount St. Joseph’s University in October 2019, Hill’s prognosis worsened this fall when scans revealed rapidly spreading Diffuse Intrinsic Pontine Glioma (DIPG). Originally given two years to live, recent imaging confirmed she has only weeks remaining. Undeterred, the former high school standout and prom queen secured a historic opportunity: the NCAA advanced Mount St. Joseph’s season opener to November 1 to allow her to play. Coach Dan Benjamin praised her selflessness and strength, noting how she prioritizes others amid her struggle. Hill expressed excitement about the game, stating, 'I can’t wait to hear the crowd roar and wear my #22 jersey.'

article_content: Nestled near Shepperton Film Studios, the 19th-century Creek House offers a rare blend of cinematic heritage and stately living space at £3 million. Once owned by TV pioneers Bernard Braden ('On The Braden Beat') and Barbara Kelly ('What's My Line?'), this seven-bedroom Georgian mansion later hosted actor John Gregson, star of Ealing comedies and the BAFTA-winning Genevieve. Architectural highlights include a vaulted stained-glass study and period-appropriate renovations revealing original fireplaces. Current owners Barry and Jane Wilkinson invested £250k over three years to restore this Thames-side property, relocating the kitchen and revitalizing gardens leading to Millbrook Creek. Unique features include a private chapel built by Thea Gregson and a storied past including Elizabeth Taylor's rumored trysts nearby. Despite strong historical appeal, current market challenges - including limited inventory and mortgage hurdles - may impact sales pace according to local agents.

article_content: A shopper at Australia's first virtual supermarket in Sydney selects products, scans barcodes from the virtual wall, pays, and has items delivered. Rising energy costs, Ukraine-related disruptions, and Middle East conflicts have strained global food systems, spurring innovation. With 8 billion people and a projected peak of 10 billion, outdated WWII-era agricultural methods must adapt to sustainability goals. Supermarkets like Migros (Turkey) and JD.com's 7Fresh leverage blockchain and AI to boost efficiency, traceability, and customer trust. While tech-driven solutions thrive in connected regions, localized initiatives are vital where online adoption lags. Balancing affordability, ethics, and scalability remains a core challenge for retailers and policymakers.

article_content: LoveAgain.com's survey of 18,000 U.S. adults uncovers regional divides in sexuality. Midwest residents claim the highest sex drive (53.5%) but only 10% have weekly intercourse—a disconnect from their reserved stereotype. Northeasterners top in frequency (25% weekly) yet have the lowest desire (43% drive). Southwest participants exhibit inflated bedroom confidence (56% men, 67% women rate themselves highly), though Texan women express dissatisfaction (42%). Western men report lowest satisfaction (32%) despite their women's strong libido (59%). Southerners overestimate their prowess (men 46%, women 39%) but engage least often (10% weekly). Nationally, 16% prioritize weekly intimacy, with Saturday preferred—except the South favoring Monday. Women (60%) outpace men (47%) in reported satisfaction, highlighting persistent gender gaps.

article_content: Government statistics reveal nearly 10% of social housing units were rented to foreign tenants during 2013/14 - up from 6% under Labour's final year in office. This marks the highest level since tracking began in 2006/7. Eastern European occupancy doubled post-2010 to 4%, coinciding with Bulgarian/Romanian EU membership. With net migration at 260,000/year, ministers admit missing targets to reduce numbers below 100,000. Proposed rules would bar recent migrants from social housing until four years' UK tax payments. Critics highlight regional disparities masking national averages, urging priority for long-term residents. While 91% of tenants are UK citizens, officials promise improved allocation processes will address inequities starting 2015/16.
